analysis.one_liner: Bars data brokers from selling people's health and location data.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to ban the sale of health and location data was introduced in July 2026 with 4 cosponsors and has sat in committee without a hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that buy and resell information about people they never collected it from — to sell or transfer health data or location data. That includes records of pregnancy, miscarriage, mental health conditions, disability, searches for health services, and even questions typed into AI chatbots, plus anything that can pinpoint where you are or were. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the ban, individuals could sue, and violators could face fines up to 15% of their parent company's annual revenue. The bill also gives the FTC $1 billion to do the work. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday people whose health and location data is currently bought and sold without their knowledge — including people seeking reproductive care, mental health treatment, or other services they would prefer to keep private. Enforcement runs through the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals' own lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose private health and location data is sold

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits data brokers from selling, licensing, trading, or transferring individuals' location data and health data, including data inferred rather than declared, and any related categories the FTC identifies [S2].

Defines health data broadly to include searches for health services, pregnancy, miscarriage, mental and physical health conditions, and information entered into AI systems, and defines location data as anything that can determine a person's past or present physical location [S2].

Gives the FTC, state attorneys general, and private individuals the power to sue violators for injunctions, deletion of data, civil penalties, and damages, with penalties capped at 15% of a violator's ultimate parent entity's annual revenue [S2].
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC to carry out the law, available through fiscal 2035 [S2].
The sale ban takes effect within 180 days of enactment, or sooner if the FTC finishes its implementing rule, and the FTC must define covered data within 180 days [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the companies that feed them data lose their ability to sell health and location information, and the Treasury pays $1 billion for enforcement. Some compliant data businesses would face costs for tracking what data they hold and deleting prohibited information, which could be passed to customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and location-based advertising businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts actions that are permissible under HIPAA rules for covered entities and business associates, so hospitals, insurers, and their contractors can still share health information under the existing (and porous) HIPAA framework; a ban on brokers narrows the market but does not close the underlying gap [S2].

Compliance could be costly: the broad definitions cover inferred data and information like AI prompts, and covered firms would have to audit, separate, and delete data categories they currently monetize, costs that could land on consumers or push some health and location services to restrict features [S2].

A private right of action with a 6-year statute of limitations running from when a plaintiff learns of the violation, and exclusive jurisdiction concentrated in D.C. courts, could produce prolonged litigation and slow remedies for individuals far from Washington [S2].
The 15%-of-revenue penalty is a ceiling, not a floor, so outcomes would depend heavily on how the FTC and courts apply it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and hard to replace: currently, data brokers can sell records that reveal a person's pregnancy, a visit to a clinic, or a daily route, and buyers have included advertisers and, in documented cases, government agencies buying location data they could not directly collect. Weighing that against the costs — compliance burdens, possible feature restrictions in health and location apps, litigation volume — the benefits appear larger for ordinary people, with the costs falling mostly on the industry that profits from the trade. The HIPAA carve-out is the most significant design gap, since it leaves the existing health-data sharing system intact for covered entities.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in July 2026 and has had no hearing, vote, or other action since; with the session running to early January 2027 it technically remains alive, but late-introduced single-party bills at this stage almost never reach the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 13, 2026, joined by Sens. Sanders, Whitehouse, and Wyden, for 4 cosponsors in total [S2][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: data brokers and the location-advertising ecosystem can continue selling health and location data while the bill sits in committee. No vote has been taken, so nothing has been decided yet; if the session ends without action, the industry is the lasting beneficiary.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers, so far — the bill sits untouched

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sens. Bernie Sanders, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Ron Wyden

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or report.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship is from the Democratic side — one Independent and three Democrats, no Republican cosponsors — and the Republican-led Commerce Committee has not acted on it.

industries.note: The bill strikes at the core of the data broker business model: buying and reselling information about people who never dealt with the company directly. Selling health and location data would become illegal, with fines up to 15% of a parent company's annual revenue. Note (plain): These companies profit by selling records of where you go and what medical care you seek, usually without you knowing.

A resale ban on location data would cut off a major supply line for targeted advertising built on people's movements. Note (plain): This industry makes money by following people's phones and selling what it learns.

industries.industry: Health apps, wearables, and AI health tools
industries.note: The bill covers health data inferred from app use and even prompts typed into AI systems, restricting a monetization path these firms use, but HIPAA-compliant and user-authorized sharing remain legal, so compliant products can keep operating. Note (plain): These companies would lose one revenue stream (selling your data onward) but could still collect and use data with your authorization.

analysis.trajectory: Introduced by a single party's members in the final months of a two-year Congress, referred to a committee with no action since, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or vote before the session ends on January 3, 2027. If nothing changes, it dies with the Congress and would need to be reintroduced in the next one.
